questions.question: Set out the legal and financial machinery of free basic water — the right, the Reserve, the allowance and its arithmetic, and how the free amount is funded.
questions.expected_answer: Section 27 of the Constitution gives everyone the right of access to sufficient water. The National Water Act of 1998 declares the nation's water a public trust managed by the state, with a Reserve set aside before any other allocation — water for basic human needs plus water to keep rivers functioning as ecosystems. The free basic water policy of 2001 converts the right into an entitlement of 6 000 litres of clean water per poor household per month, derived from 25 litres per person per day for an assumed household of eight over a month, with policy adding that the supply point should stand within 200 metres of the home. Twenty-five litres covers only drinking, cooking and basic hygiene, against roughly 150 litres a day used by a plumbed suburban resident, so the allowance is a floor, not comfort. Because water must be stored, piped, purified and pumped, the free amount is funded from national grants and from the rising block tariff: monthly consumption is priced in steps, the first block free or nearly free and each further block more expensive per litre, so frugal households stay in the cheap blocks while heavy users pay rates that discourage waste and cross-subsidise the basic allowance. Finally, access must be distinguished from delivery: a distant shared standpipe or a connection to a failed pump still counts as access on paper.

questions.question: Contrast the rural and urban obstacles to water delivery in South Africa, and identify the institutional weakness underlying both.
questions.expected_answer: Rural delivery struggles with dispersal across distance: in the former homeland regions of the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo, small settlements scatter over vast rugged terrain, so each kilometre of pipe serves few households and the cost per connection multiplies in the very regions historic neglect left furthest behind. Sources are fragile — small dams, springs and boreholes that fail in drought — and the maintenance trap completes the cycle: schemes built with capital grants break, and small municipalities without engineers or revenue cannot repair them, so villages return to rivers. The burden lands on women and girls, who fetch water over kilometres at a cost in schooling and safety, and shared, contaminated water brings diseases including cholera. Urban delivery fails differently: cities grow faster than pipes, so informal settlements form on unserviced land — often floodplains and steep slopes — relying on shared standpipes; unemployment leaves many unable to pay, feeding disputes over billing and disconnection; and a third or more of treated water is non-revenue, lost to burst mains, faulty meters and unbilled use, meaning a city must treat roughly three litres to sell two, with theft and vandalism adding further losses. Beneath both geographies lies the same institutional illness: municipalities short of money, skills and maintenance discipline, so infrastructure decays and access statistics conceal dry taps.

questions.question: Explain the gravity logic of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project against its pumped alternative, list the five purification steps in order, and use Cape Town and Nelson Mandela Bay to argue the two-sided nature of sustainable water use.
questions.expected_answer: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project rests on two facts: the Lesotho highlands catch the region's heaviest rain and snow, and they stand far above Gauteng. Dams at Katse and Mohale — with Polihali under construction — capture the water at its source, and tunnels through the mountains let it flow northward into the Vaal system entirely by gravity, with Lesotho earning royalties among its largest national incomes plus hydro-electricity. The Tugela-Vaal scheme performs the same service against the grain, pumping Thukela water up the escarpment into Sterkfontein Dam at a heavy electricity cost, which is why Sterkfontein is held as a drought reserve; the Orange-Fish Tunnel sends Gariep water south to Eastern Cape irrigation. Purification runs through five steps: screening removes coarse debris; coagulation and flocculation bind fine dirt into flocs; sedimentation settles the flocs in calm tanks; filtration through sand and gravel removes remaining particles; disinfection with chlorine, sometimes ozone or ultraviolet, kills pathogens — with Blue Drop auditing drinking water and Green Drop auditing sewage works. The two cities then prove sustainability has two role-players: Cape Town, facing Day Zero in 2018, roughly halved daily use from above a thousand million litres toward five hundred million through disciplined household savings, restrictions and tariffs, and kept its taps open; Nelson Mandela Bay's drought into 2022, met with late savings and unfixed leaks, dragged on for years. The state must fix pipes, protect quality, clear invasive plants, price wisely and diversify sources; citizens must mend leaks, shower short, harvest rain, reuse greywater and obey restrictions — neither half succeeds alone.
